2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). cross_tool_domains.attrition: Moderate concern / Can't tell: Single-visit cross-sectional data collection had no longitudinal loss to follow-up, but 3 of 30 interviewed participants (10%) yielded unusable Q-sorts and were excluded without reporting the reasons for exclusion or their neighbourhood profiles; additionally, 3 of the 27 usable Q-sorts did not load significantly on the five retained factors.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern (uncontrolled exploratory design): Observational Q-methodology study with no comparator arm or statistical confounder adjustment; neighbourhood, historical racialised segregation, occupation, household size and water bill levels co-vary in small subsamples (e.g. all Factor 2 respondents worked at one Mitchells Plain school), and the authors explicitly state the study cannot verify causal relationships.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate (contextual and normative operationalisation): Cape Town's municipal water governance instruments (increasing block tariffs, the 6,000 L/month free basic water threshold, indigent registration rules, Water Management Devices [WMDs] and the 2020 Water Strategy) are accurately contextualised from municipal and secondary sources and operationalised into 25 normative tariff-design statements, though formal municipal tariff by-laws are not doctrinally coded as an empirical treatment variable.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate concern: Subjective tariff fairness viewpoints were elicited using a piloted 25-statement Q-set with positively and negatively worded items on a forced quasi-normal grid (-4 to +4), mitigating acquiescence bias; however, household income and monthly water costs relied on unverified self-report (with several City Bowl respondents unaware of their bill size), language/translation procedures across multilingual neighbourhoods are unreported and post-sort qualitative explanations are not presented verbatim.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate: Subjective fairness perspectives are rigorously structured via Q-sort rankings and principal component analysis with varimax rotation (retaining 5 factors at p < 0.01 explaining 61% of sample variance), whereas physical/economic water outcomes are limited to categorical self-reported monthly water bills (Fig. 3) and qualitative rationales lack direct participant quotations.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern: No pre-analysis protocol or registration is reported; quantitative ideal-sort scores and statistical significance markers for all 25 statements across all 5 retained factors are fully reported in Table 1 (with transparent criteria for dropping 3 single-sort factors), but qualitative post-sort interview data are selectively absent from the Results.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern: Non-probability convenience sampling via personal and professional networks supplemented by divergent-viewpoint snowball sampling across three neighbourhoods (n = 30 interviewed, n = 27 usable Q-sorts); while purposive diversity aligns with Q-methodology aims, initial recruitment refusal rates are unreported and notable workplace/occupational clustering occurred (all 4 Factor 2 respondents worked at the same school in Mitchells Plain; Factor 3 skewed heavily toward affluent professionals).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Screening S1: Are there clear research questions?
domain_ratings.justification: The paper clearly states its aim to investigate subjective perceptions of fairness regarding Cape Town's post-drought water tariffs across residents in three distinct socioeconomic contexts, examining distributive, procedural and interactional justice dimensions.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Screening S2: Do the collected data allow to address the research questions?
domain_ratings.justification: Collecting 27 usable 25-statement Q-sorts alongside household demographic and water-cost characteristics across City Bowl, Mitchells Plain and Dunoon directly enables identification and comparison of distinct subjective perspectives on fair water tariffs.
domain_ratings.where_found: Methodology (PDF pp. 4-7); Results, Table 1 & Fig. 3 (PDF pp. 6-8)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.1: Is the qualitative approach appropriate to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Qualitative concourse generation (from media, municipal meetings, online forums and key informants) combined with structured crib-sheet discourse interpretation is appropriate for exploring contested subjective meanings of fairness in water governance.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.2: Are the qualitative data collection methods adequate to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Statement compilation continued to saturation (~40 statements piloted down to 25) and respondents were interviewed individually; however, the paper does not report whether open-ended post-sort probing questions were asked, whether interviews were audio-recorded/transcribed, interview duration or what languages were used in multilingual areas (Dunoon and Mitchells Plain).
domain_ratings.where_found: Statements for the Q-sorts & Participant selection and data collection (PDF p. 5)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.3: Are the findings adequately derived from the data?
domain_ratings.justification: Factor arrays (Table 1) were systematically interpreted using the established qualitative crib-sheet technique (Watts and Stenner 2012; West et al. 2016) to identify distinguishing, consensus and extreme-ranked statements for each of the five perspectives.
domain_ratings.where_found: Analysis and interpretation (PDF pp. 6-7); Results (PDF pp. 7-10)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.4: Is the interpretation of results sufficiently substantiated by data?
domain_ratings.justification: While the five factor narratives are transparently anchored to statement rankings in Table 1 and household attributes in Fig. 3, zero verbatim qualitative quotes from respondent interviews are provided to substantiate why participants ranked statements as they did, and neighbourhood-level historical explanations in the Discussion rely heavily on secondary literature rather than participant testimony.
domain_ratings.where_found: Results (PDF pp. 7-10); Discussion: Interactional justice (PDF pp. 11-12)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.5: Is there coherence between qualitative data sources, collection, analysis and interpretation?
domain_ratings.justification: There is clear conceptual coherence linking Cape Town's institutional/tariff context, concourse development, factor crib-sheet narratives and the distributive, procedural and interactional justice framework, with explicit caveats against overclaiming causality or population generalisability.
domain_ratings.where_found: Introduction (PDF pp. 2-3); Methodology (PDF pp. 4-7); Discussion (PDF pp. 10-12)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative descriptive 4.1: Is the sampling strategy relevant to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Purposively recruiting participants across three historically and socioeconomically contrasting Cape Town neighbourhoods (City Bowl, Mitchells Plain and Dunoon) via initial convenience networks plus divergent-viewpoint snowball sampling fits Q-methodology's objective of capturing diverse subjective viewpoints.
domain_ratings.where_found: Participant selection and data collection (PDF p. 5); Fig. 1 (PDF p. 3)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative descriptive 4.2: Is the sample representative of the target population?
domain_ratings.justification: As the authors explicitly note, the small convenience and snowball sample (30 interviewed, 27 usable Q-sorts) is not statistically representative of Cape Town's population; notable clustering occurred (e.g. all four Factor 2 respondents worked at a single school in Mitchells Plain, and municipal water officials were not included).
domain_ratings.where_found: Methodology (PDF pp. 4-5); Results (PDF pp. 7-9); Discussion (PDF p. 12)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative descriptive 4.3: Are the measurements appropriate?
domain_ratings.justification: The 25-statement Q-set was piloted to remove overlap and simplify wording across educational levels, balanced with positively and negatively framed items and ranked on a standard forced quasi-normal 9-column Q-grid (-4 to +4), supplemented by basic household size, income and water-bill indicators.
domain_ratings.where_found: Statements for the Q-sorts & Participant selection and data collection, Fig. 2 & Table 1 (PDF pp. 5-6)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative descriptive 4.4: Is the risk of nonresponse bias low?
domain_ratings.justification: The number of prospective participants invited who declined to participate during convenience and snowball recruitment is not reported, and 3 of 30 completed interviews produced unusable Q-sorts without disclosure of why they were unusable or which neighbourhoods they came from.
domain_ratings.where_found: Participant selection and data collection (PDF p. 5)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative descriptive 4.5: Is the statistical analysis appropriate to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Using PQMethod, the authors computed intercorrelations across all 27 Q-sorts, conducted principal component analysis with varimax rotation, applied an explicit p < 0.01 factor-loading cut-off of ±0.516 (2.58 × 1/√25), eliminated single-respondent factors and identified statistically significant distinguishing and consensus statements.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed methods 5.1: Is there an adequate rationale for using a mixed methods design to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors justify Q-methodology specifically for its capacity to combine statistically structured quantitative factor extraction with qualitative discourse analysis to bring initial coherence to contested subjective perceptions of tariff fairness.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed methods 5.2: Are the different components of the study effectively integrated to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Quantitative PCA factor arrays and significance tests (Table 1) and household socioeconomic/water-cost profiles (Fig. 3) are directly integrated with qualitative crib-sheet interpretation to construct and contextualise the five fairness personas.
domain_ratings.where_found: Analysis and interpretation & Results, Table 1, Fig. 3 & Fig. 4 (PDF pp. 6-10)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed methods 5.3: Are the outputs of the integration of qualitative and quantitative components adequately interpreted?
domain_ratings.justification: The integrated outputs (the Insurer, Individualist, Bureaucrat, Humanitarian and Prepper viewpoints) are thoughtfully interpreted through distributive, procedural, interactional and intergenerational justice lenses while explicitly acknowledging non-causality and hypothesis-generating scope.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed methods 5.4: Are divergences and inconsistencies between quantitative results and qualitative findings adequately addressed?
domain_ratings.justification: Counterintuitive and cross-cutting findings—such as working-class Mitchells Plain respondents with high water bills opposing pro-poor redistribution (Factor 2), internal tension within Factor 5 on social versus scarcity goals and Factors 1 and 5 cutting across all neighbourhoods and income levels—are explicitly discussed.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed methods 5.5: Do the different components of the study adhere to the quality criteria of each tradition of the methods involved?
domain_ratings.justification: While Q-sort construction and PCA/varimax statistical procedures follow established Q-methodology conventions, the qualitative component lacks verbatim post-sort interview evidence, researcher reflexivity/positionality and reported ethics/informed-consent procedures, and the quantitative sample exhibits convenience/workplace clustering and unreported nonresponse.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Enqvist and van Oyen (2023) employ Q-methodology—an inherently mixed-methods ('qualiquantological') design combining qualitative concourse generation and crib-sheet discourse interpretation with quantitative forced-grid ranking and principal component analysis (PCA)—to explore subjective perceptions of water tariff fairness across three socioeconomically and historically distinct Cape Town neighbourhoods (City Bowl, Mitchells Plain and Dunoon) 1 year after the 2015–2018 drought. Appraised using the MMAT (2018), the study demonstrates strong conceptual coherence, careful piloting of a 25-statement Q-set, transparent PCA/varimax factor extraction (p < 0.01 loading threshold of ±0.516; 5 multi-respondent factors explaining 61% of variance), effective integration of factor arrays with household socioeconomic profiles and measured interpretation that explicitly avoids causal or population-representative claims. Methodological concerns stem from convenience and snowball sampling (30 interviewed, 27 usable Q-sorts) with pronounced workplace clustering (all four 'Individualist' Factor 2 respondents worked at a single school in Mitchells Plain), unreported initial refusal rates and reasons for excluding 3 unusable Q-sorts, absence of verbatim post-sort qualitative interview quotes to substantiate why respondents ranked statements as they did (leaving historical/interactional explanations reliant on secondary literature) and lack of reported ethical approval/consent or researcher reflexivity across multilingual, highly unequal study sites. Per MMAT 2018 guidance, no numeric composite score is computed; overall quality reflects moderate methodological concern bounded by these sampling and qualitative reporting limitations.
raw_response.overall_rating: Moderate methodological concern (strong Q-set piloting, PCA factor analysis, and qual-quant integration, bounded by convenience/snowball sampling with single-workplace clustering, unreported recruitment nonresponse and 3/30 excluded sorts, absence of verbatim post-sort interview evidence, and unreported ethics/reflexivity)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Mixed-methods Q-methodology study (combining qualitative concourse development, individual sorting interviews, and crib-sheet discourse interpretation with quantitative forced quasi-normal Q-sort rankings, principal component analysis with varimax rotation, and descriptive household socioeconomic profiling; n = 30 interviewed, 27 usable Q-sorts)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Abstract (PDF p. 1); Introduction (PDF pp. 2-3); Past and present patterns of injustice (PDF pp. 3-4); Methodology: Statements for the Q-sorts, Participant selection and data collection, Analysis and interpretation (PDF pp. 4-7); Results, Table 1, Fig. 3 & Fig. 4 (PDF pp. 6-10); Discussion (PDF pp. 10-12).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The study uses primary Q-methodology, which explicitly combines qualitative empirical methods (concourse generation via documentary/forum review and key-informant conversations, individual sorting interviews and qualitative crib-sheet interpretation) with quantitative descriptive methods (numerical relative ranking of 25 statements on a -4 to +4 quasi-normal grid, intercorrelation matrix, principal component analysis with varimax rotation, statistical significance testing of factor loadings and distinguishing/consensus statements and descriptive household water-bill/income profiling). Because both qualitative and quantitative descriptive empirical components are core and integrated to produce the study's findings, MMAT (with the Quantitative Descriptive 4.1-4.5 block) is the exact matching appraisal tool.
